statement: Two squares, each with side length $6$, overlap so that the region they share is a rectangle $2$ wide and $6$ long. What is the area of the region covered by at least one of the two squares?

choices.misconception: I found the area of the shared rectangle, 2 times 6 = 12, instead of the area covered by at least one square.
I subtracted the shared rectangle from both squares, 72 - 2 times 12 = 48, which is the area covered by exactly one square.
I added the two square areas, 36 + 36 = 72, which counts the shared rectangle twice.
I added the shared rectangle to the two squares, 72 + 12 = 84, instead of subtracting it.

hints: Adding the areas of the two squares counts part of the region twice. Which part?
The shared $2$ by $6$ rectangle is inside both squares, so $36 + 36$ counts it twice.

solutions.reliable: Each square has area $6^2 = 36$, so together they have area $72$, but the shared rectangle, with area $2 \cdot 6 = 12$, is counted in both. Counting it only once, the covered region has area $36 + 36 - 12 = 60$.
solutions.elegant: The shared rectangle is a full $6$ long, so the squares sit side by side, shifted $6 - 2 = 4$ units apart. Together they form a $6$ by $10$ rectangle, with area $6 \cdot 10 = 60$.

author: Devansh Sanghavi
